A phase that only reproduces a published number, or only measures throughput the question does not ask about, does not count. Give decides_by_reason in at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Root question: What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?
Option record: {\"id\":\"I1\",\"title\":\"Drift probes on the autoformalizer\",\"summary\":\"Probe the autoformalizer's activations while it writes definitions and statements, to flag when it has quietly strengthened a hypothesis or guessed a convention. In math, generators often 'know' they are wrong: a linear probe predicts trace correctness at 0.953 AUROC on MATH-500, against 0.674 for verbalized confidence. But transfer to other domains is weak (0.54/0.55 from MATH to ARC), the signal is 'diagnostic, not causal', and the only interp study of autoformalization (SMT-LIB, not Lean) gets 0.960 against a solver oracle but 0.679 against an LLM proxy for intent. No one has measured this on Lean, and the labels it needs are the human audit itself.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether a misformalization of the root statement or its definitions, which the kernel cannot see, leaves a readable trace inside the generator, which would shrink the human audit set.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models and labelled statements analysed. The most reported is nine models up to 72B on 100 training and 200 held-out math problems (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09502v1) and 950 SMT-LIB encodings (https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11085v2). Unknown above that: whether Lean statement drift is linearly readable in any model at all, and how a probe scores against human rather than solver or LLM-proxy intent labels.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert-labelled faithful/unfaithful pairs, then one forward pass per statement to cache activations, then a probe fit (minutes on a fraction of one GPU), then held-out evaluation. That is about 4 steps, with one run per model and realistically per subfield. Only the labelling step is serial (it is the expert audit). Labels could arrive in parallel if faithful statements were perturbed synthetically in targeted directions, as BPF's counterfactual probe generation does (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16541). That pays off only if probes trained on synthetic drift transfer to natural misformalizations. The nearest precedent is Goodfire's Rakuten SAE probes, trained on synthetic data, which held up on real production data (https://www.goodfire.com/research/rakuten-sae-probes-for-pii-detection).\",\"source_urls\":[\"https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09502v1\",\"https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11085v2\",\"https://arxiv.org/html/2504.05419v1\"]}

card:question: Can a linear probe read Lean autoformalization drift from generator activations, and does synthetic-drift training transfer to human-audited natural misformalizations?
card:hypothesis: Generators encode drift they cannot verbalize: a linear probe predicts trace correctness at 0.953, so Lean misformalizations should be linearly readable.
card:sequential_part: Expert-labelled faithful/drifted pairs, one forward pass per statement, probe fit, held-out evaluation — four steps.
card:method: Synthetic drift is generated in parallel by counterfactual perturbation, and forward passes over many statements run side-by-side on separate GPUs.
card:if_lever: Synthetic-drift probes transfer to natural Lean misformalizations: parallel GPUs reach AUROC ≥ 0.80 at 5,000 statement-runs, sooner than one sequential GPU.
card:if_not: Drift is weakly readable in Lean: probe AUROC on natural misformalizations stays near 0.679 even at 150,000 statement-runs, so it never crosses the flagging threshold.
card:test_summary: Cache a 7B Lean autoformalizer's hidden states over 100k+ runs; train logistic probes on synthetic drift, test on 200 human-audited natural misformalizations; time parallel 4-GPU vs sequential and sharded-copy baselines; compare AUROC to SMT-LIB 0.960/0.679.
card:closest_prior: A linear SAE probe reached 0.960 AUROC against an SMT-LIB solver oracle but 0.679 against intent labels; largest compute: 950 encodings, one 27B verifier.
card:left_open: No one has measured drift readability in Lean (only SMT-LIB), scored a probe against human audit labels, or tested synthetic-to-natural drift transfer.
card:anchor: Planted synthetic-drift probe hits AUROC ≥ 0.90; 4-shard parallel caching matches single-GPU sequential caching within ±0.05 AUROC; shuffle control 0.50.
card:limits: Shows readability, not a causal fix, and only within Lean. Cannot prove synthetic-to-natural transfer beyond the audited 200 pairs.

Criteria:
stakes: Take the two outcomes this test predicts, as measured here and within the limits in scope_gap. 5 = whichever occurs, a choice someone faces (what to buy, build, collect or scale next) changes, and the test measures the quantity that choice depends on; 3 = the outcomes bear on that choice only through a step this test does not check (a stand-in system, simulation to reality, a single model), or one outcome is already much more likely than the other; 1 = neither outcome would change anything. Do not score how famous the field is or how close it is to the root question.
lever: Could the result tell if_lever from if_not, with compute the only thing that changed? Check four conditions: (a) the predicted difference between if_lever and if_not is larger than what noise_rule says run-to-run noise can produce; (b) compute_axis spans at least 10×; (c) the varied quantity is bought with compute, not with more data, labels or people (when restructuring.method is not none: the arms run on the same hardware and differ only in method); (d) inputs that could also explain the difference are in held_fixed. 5 = all four hold; 3 = one fails or cannot be told from the plan; 1 = two or more fail, or the measured quantity is not the one the question asks about.
verifiable: What is the measured outcome scored against? 5 = an exact or planted truth that does not come from the method under test (a simulation's hidden true run, an exact success flag, a formal checker, planted items), and the setup first reproduces a published number within a stated tolerance; 3 = labels from a model or human rater with an agreement check, or exact truth with no reproduction step; 1 = nothing independent of the method's own output.
open: Does the closest published result already answer this question over this range? 5 = the quoted prior stops short of this range or asks a different question, and the plan states the gap; 3 = the prior answers part of it (a narrower range, a related system), or no prior is named; 1 = the quoted prior already answers it. Reusing published tools, models or benchmarks does not lower this score.
internals: Does the test compare the internals readout with the strongest outputs-only method named in the plan or the option, on the same items, with a numeric margin in decision_rule? 5 = yes; 3 = compares only with a weaker outputs-only method than one named, or gives no margin; 1 = no outputs-only comparison.
reshape: Does the plan remove a step-after-step dependency that one answer waits on, rather than run independent work side by side? 5 = restructuring names the dependency, why it need not run in order and how the plan computes it at the same time; condition says what must hold for that to pay off; condition_phase measures it before the main spend; and the closest prior does not already do this for this system; 3 = it removes a dependency, but condition is missing or is not measured before the main spend; 2 = it parallelises only within each step (splitting a large state across GPUs) or regroups and rebalances independent work (batching unfinished runs, load balancing, lower precision), leaving the chain in order; 1 = independent copies side by side, or one job per GPU, is the only parallelism, or the plan rebuilds a parallel version the closest prior already reports for this system. baseline: Is the gain timed against the strongest ways to get the same answer without the plan's method?
